title: Stees v. Leonard
summary: A builder’s undertaking to erect and complete a building placed the burden of overcoming the site’s quicksand conditions on the builder under the court’s strict reading of the contract.
notes: The editors contrast United States v. Spearin and distinguish a specification requiring a result from a detailed design that may imply a warranty of adequacy. That later contrast qualifies the use of Stees as a general construction-risk rule.

sections.Parties: Stees and the other plaintiffs owned the building site. Leonard and the other defendants undertook to construct and complete the building according to attached plans and specifications.
sections.Material Facts:
The builders twice carried construction to a height of three stories, and the building collapsed both times. They then refused to proceed. They attributed the collapses to quicksand that could not support the building when water entered it, and maintained that they had followed the plans and specifications. Those specifications prescribed foundation-wall and footing dimensions without otherwise specifying the foundations’ character.

The owners alleged negligent work and poor materials and sought recovery of payments made, loss of use of the lot, and damage to adjacent property. The builders sought to prove a prior oral agreement that the owners would drain the site. They also offered evidence of later drainage promises.
sections.Procedural History: A jury found for the owners. The trial court denied the builders’ motion for a new trial. The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed, including the exclusion of the offered drainage evidence.
sections.Issue: Did unexpected soil problems excuse the builders’ failure to complete, and could the claimed oral drainage undertakings shift the responsibility?
sections.Holding: No excuse or effective transfer of the drainage responsibility was established. The builders remained responsible for the performance they expressly undertook.
sections.Reasoning:
The court read the completion promise broadly: if stronger foundations or drainage were necessary to erect the building, those measures were within the builders’ obligation. Compliance with the stated footing specifications therefore did not establish performance of the larger promise. The opinion emphasized the possibility of negotiating a qualified undertaking instead of assuming an absolute one.

The prior oral drainage promise concerned work the court considered embraced by the written agreement, so the court excluded it under the parol evidence rule. The later promises were also excluded because the builders had not alleged consideration or justifiable reliance sufficient to support them. Those procedural and pleading limits matter to the apparent allocation of risk.

This is a historical strict-liability approach to the construction undertaking. The surrounding materials contrast owner-provided design specifications and later excuse doctrines; the opinion should not be turned into a universal rule that every contractor assumes every defect in an owner’s design.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Stees establishes the background expectation that a party bears the risks its promise allocates. It connects the definition of the promised result, parol evidence, modification, and excuse.

topics.mistake: Unexpected site conditions did not free the builders from the broad completion obligation as construed.
topics.impracticability: Difficulty and added measures did not establish an excuse under the court’s strict approach.
topics.risk-allocation: The completion promise allocated the necessary foundations and drainage work to the builders.
topics.parol-evidence: A prior oral drainage undertaking was excluded because it concerned a subject included in the written obligation.
topics.modification: Later drainage promises lacked the pleaded support the court required.

mnemonic.rationale: A building that sank into quicksand
